question: Since the diabetes medicine containing the active substance semaglutide was found to be effective in inducing weight loss and suppressing appetite, its sales have sky-rocketed, increasing by 58 % on an annual basis, as has its price. As a result, there have been numerous phishing incidents with fake websites advertising the medicine and luring unsuspecting victims with low prices.

Victims are asked to fill out a form with personal information such as their name, address and bank account details. It is difficult to tell the difference between a fake and a genuine retail website so consumers can easily be scammed1. In view of this: 1.
Has the Commission received any complaints about scam websites given that the phenomenon is not only limited to Greece?
What steps will it take to ensure that citizens are promptly informed and to prevent them falling victim to scams?
answer: Different cases of online scams have been reported to the Commission by actors such as the national consumer authorities in the Consumer Protection Cooperation Network and the European Consumer Centres Network. In 2024, 45% of consumers in the EU encountered online scams over the previous 12 months.

(2) While enforcement of the Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU and the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive 2005/29/EC lies primarily with Member States, the Commission coordinates cross-border enforcement under the Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) Regulation (EU) 2017/2394 (3) to tackle widespread breaches of EU consumer law.

The European Multidisciplinary Platform Against Criminal Threats (4) also targets organised crime, including fraud, through investigations, prevention and partnerships (5). As announced in the European Internal Security Strategy Communication (6), the Commission plans to present an Action Plan on Online Fraud in 2026, focusing on prevention and enforcement.

The Digital Services Act (DSA) requires designated very large online platforms to assess systemic risks, including online scams, and to implement mitigation measures. The Commission is also preparing a Digital Fairness Act (DFA) (7), which, subject to an impact assessment, may introduce stricter rules on practices such as misleading influencer marketing and exploitative personalisation.
Finally, the European Consumer Centres Network supports awareness-raising campaigns like EU Safer Internet Days to promote online safety and a fair digital environment.
